webTitle: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters

fields.headline: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
fields.trailText: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
fields.bodyText: The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil. Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world. The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government. On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait. The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating. “We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said. The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result. “Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump. As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly. The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance. Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan. The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending. Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur. Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer. They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks. Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting. Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday. Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality. Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.” Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home. Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy. On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said. Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture … “To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.” Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming. The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration. Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.

webTitle: Trump set to press Zelenskyy at UN to agree to energy ceasefire with Russia

fields.headline: Trump set to press Zelenskyy at UN to agree to energy ceasefire with Russia
fields.trailText: US president to meet Ukrainian counterpart in New York as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian energy sector
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people. On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine. “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truths Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.” “This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!” Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities. Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”. “Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.” The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. The Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with the secretary of state, Marco Rubio. During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”. “Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said. Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”. Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November. Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez. In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.” Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed upon, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued.

webTitle: Key ally urges Trump to back US farmers amid anger over rising prices

fields.headline: Key ally urges Trump to back US farmers amid anger over rising prices
fields.trailText: Iowa senator Chuck Grassley calls for embargo on diesel exports as tariffs and Iran war drive up costs for sector
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump is facing growing calls, including from within his own party, to boost support for US farmers as his administration faces mounting anger over its treatment of the agricultural sector. Republican senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa called on the US president to place an embargo on diesel exports this weekend and help farmers grapple with high prices. Grassley, who is largely aligned with Trump, suggested the embargo in multiple social media posts, calling on the president to issue a 1970s-style embargo on diesel and agricultural products to help farmers. “If our [government] can embargo chips to China it can embargo diesel to help American farmers & truckers,” Grassley wrote on Sunday. “We need our family farmers who feed&fuel the world [to be] on the strongest footing possible no matter what’s happening across the globe.” For months, farmers – traditionally a reliable Republican voting base – have been angry with the Trump administration because they believe some of its policies adversely affect them. That includes tariffs, which have driven up the cost of fertilizer, machine parts, seed and more; increasing beef imports to lower prices for Americans, which undermines domestic producers; and the Iran war, which has made it more expensive for farmers to operate machinery and transport products. The national average cost of diesel was $6.51 as of Sunday, according to AAA. In Iowa, it was slightly lower at $6.31 – still nearly $3 more than the cost one year ago. Gas prices are not the only rising cost Americans are facing as a result of the Iran war. Groceries have also become more expensive, and the Trump administration has sought to lower some of those prices, particularly beef, by allowing 300,000 metric tons of overseas beef trimmings to enter the US at a reduced tariff rate. But domestic farmers in the US, who are already struggling with smaller herds, say the decision will increase competition and make it more difficult to sell their own. “It takes something big to change long-established voting patterns, but I think there’s a possibility that the Trump administration has done things that are big enough and bad enough from the standpoint of rural America to make some of the voters who shifted a decade ago reconsider their choice,” William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told the Washington Sun. Ryan Marquardt, the vice-president of the Iowa Farmers Union, told the Washington Sun he had “never seen farmers more pissed” than when Trump raised the imports of foreign beef. Farmers’ outrage toward the Trump administration has worried Republican politicians, such as Grassley, whose base includes farmers and rural voters. As November’s midterms approach, some politicians closely aligned with farmers have publicly broken with Trump, while others have sought ways to adjust the president’s policies. Iowa congresswoman Ashley Hinson, historically a Trump ally, recently adjusted her campaign strategy to highlight her work across the aisle and has repeatedly voiced opposition to the president’s tariff policies that have affected farmers. When asked by the Gazette, an Iowa newspaper, whether a vote for her would be a vote for Trump last week, Hinson replied: “I vote for me is a vote for commonsense policies, and no matter who is in the White House. That’s what I’m going to focus on.” Grassley, meanwhile, suggested an embargo on diesel, akin to the Trump administration’s embargo on semiconductor chips – though that specific embargo was considered national-security related. When asked for comment, the White House pointed to statements from interior secretary Doug Burgum and executive director of the national energy dominance council, Jarrod Agen, at a G20 meeting in Houston earlier this month. Agen and Burgum dismissed the possibility of implementing a ban on diesel, gasoline or crude oil. “We would consider an export ban if we thought that actually might lower prices, but that’s not the case,” Burgum told reporters. Brooke Rollins, the US agriculture secretary, told reporters on Monday that Trump had called her earlier in the day to discuss the issue of diesel for farmers and that Americans could “expect an announcement very soon on some potential actions”. “It is the direct result, clearly, of the Iran war,” Rollins acknowledged, arguing that the short term “implications” were “not easy”, but necessary, to ensure that Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026. An earlier version said Doug Burgum was the energy secretary; in fact, he is the interior secretary.

webTitle: Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute

fields.headline: Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute
fields.trailText: US president reportedly changed his mind over Saudi Arabia’s pleas for assistance as bombs were being loaded
fields.bodyText: Houthi fighters are moving to seize strategic heights in Yemen that would cut the Red Sea coast off from areas held by Saudi-backed forces after Donald Trump called off US strikes on the group at the last minute, reportedly as bombs were being loaded on to aircraft. Amid increasingly heavy fighting in Yemen, which has displaced tens of thousands of people in recent weeks, the New York Times reported on Monday that the US president had flip-flopped wildly in recent days after a call from Saudi Arabia for US strikes on the Houthis. It comes amid the Houthis’ rapid advance on the ground with the group gaining control over much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and advancing to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. In the call reported by the New York Times, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, implored Trump to step in to help halt the Houthi advance after weeks of such appeals. Trump, who had been resisting joining the Saudi war in Yemen, after the call then told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis before reversing course once again, the report said. Trump has frequently given mixed signals to Riyadh, telling reporters during a visit to Ireland earlier this month that the Houthis “called us, and they don’t want to fight us”, adding that the group was “allowing ships to pass” the Bab al-Mandab strait and that the situation would “work out very well”. He added that the Houthi problem was limited to “one country” an apparent reference to Saudi Arabia promising to “take care of fixing that”. The UN says hostilities in Yemen have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September. Taiz city has received the largest number of displaced persons, taking in up to 86,000 Yemenis since the recent escalation began. The rapid advance by the Iran-aligned group this ‌month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies. Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Prince Mohammed to join the fight in Yemen with the Houthis claiming on Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where columns of smoke were visible near the main airport. The Yemeni president, ⁠Rashad al-Alimi, ⁠spoke to Trump on Sunday, requesting ‌support for his ‌UN-recognised government in its fight against the Houthis. Trump ⁠made no direct pledge of military support during the call, sources said. Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on Houthi positions in the strategic Kahboub mountains, according to the group, but making little impact on the advance of its fighters. Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast, which separate the Red Sea coast from the city of Aden, where the government is based. The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab strait by taking control of the mountains, which would also allow them to open new ‌fronts, according to ⁠sources who spoke to Reuters. The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has created a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran. The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since. Amid the broad failure of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and with the US midterm elections looming, the Trump administration’s priorities appear to be to secure at least some oil supplies through the strait of Hormuz, while avoiding a wider entanglement in Yemen. That, however, invites longer-term risks, not least the growing alienation of key US allies in the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia, where Washington is increasingly seen as an unreliable ally, that could also undermine the so-called “security for oil” understanding where the US provides a defence umbrella for Gulf states in exchange for energy supplies. Reuters contributed to this report

webTitle: Mark Carney is making an eloquent case for an alliance sidelining the US | Ted Widmer

fields.headline: Mark Carney is making an eloquent case for an alliance sidelining the US
fields.trailText: The Canadian prime minister’s remarks before the European parliament outlined a vision of the west without its most powerful member
fields.bodyText: The speeches keep coming, each building on the previous one, as the Canadian prime minister builds a case for a new world order that has strikingly little to do with the United States of America, the country that has led the west since the second world war. On 20 January, in Davos, Mark Carney proposed that the world’s middle powers do more to support each other, in light of a “rupture” in the global order. That was clearly a reference to the destabilizing policies of Donald Trump, who had been inaugurated exactly one year earlier, and had spent most of that year insulting the US’s allies. On Thursday, before the European parliament in Strasbourg, Carney delivered another powerful oration that outlined what a new west might look like, without its most powerful member. In his speech, Carney signaled his desire to build bridges across the Atlantic at a time when the US-Canadian relationship is badly strained over trade disputes and Donald Trump’s kindergarten taunts. The EU has offered to make Canada an “associate member”, and while it is unclear what that means (the EU has no such category), it’s a depressing sign that the US’s historic allies are seeking new solutions for a world in which they can no longer trust the United States – for 80 years, the bulwark of the alliance. That this was a blow to American prestige was immediately evident from Trump’s angry reaction on social media: he called the idea “laughable” and threatened, as always, to impose more tariffs. That will only accelerate the growing trend to pay no attention to him. In contrast, Carney expressed himself with seriousness and purpose. He began in French, thanking his hosts, then went confidently into Europe’s fraught history, exploring ambitious themes that are central to the continent’s identity. He quoted Goethe, and in German no less. The words (from Faust) were memorable: Nur der verdient sich Freiheit wie das Leben, der täglich sie erobern muß (“Freedom and life must be earned every single day”). With surgical precision, he then applied that thought to specific episodes in the 20th century, including the failed Hungarian revolution of 1956 (when Russian tanks crushed a people’s dream of freedom), and 1989, when the Berlin Wall came down, and the Iron Curtain finally began to crumble. It was impressive to hear a world leader with a command of history, exploring both the failures and the successes of the past, before a knowledgeable audience. Hungary remains on the front lines of freedom, having voted out the odious Viktor Orbán in April. Carney offered knowing references to the first world war, a conflict that Canadians remember more vividly than Americans do (they entered the war in 1914, three years earlier than the US, and suffered more casualties). He is also drawn to natural imagery; a moving story described a young Canadian soldier who gathered acorns from a French battlefield during the first world war, then planted them in Ontario, where they grew into a “majestic forest”. Today grafts from these Canadian oaks are being replanted at the original battlefield, completing “a profound circle of renewal”. That language would be difficult to imagine in a speech by the US president, who cut down a historic tree on the White House campus, paved the Rose Garden’s lawn, and generally avoids references to nature, unless they involve golf. He also disdains history. In 2018, 100 years after the first world war ended, Trump raised hackles during a visit to France, when he refused to visit a cemetery of US war dead, out of concern that a helicopter flight would affect his hair. The Atlantic reported at the time that he had also dismissed the US war dead as “suckers” and “losers”. Carney went out of his way to say that the new EU-Canadian rapport did not stem from a desire to “dominate others” or seek to become a new great-power rival to those that already exist. But even as he expressed his values, there was a tone of defiance. Repeatedly, Carney stressed the issue of “sovereignty”, and it was not difficult to draw the lesson that Canadians and Europeans remain aghast over Trump’s longstanding fixation on Greenland. Canadians are also furious over the president’s repeated claim that he will make Canada – a larger country than the United States – the “51st state”. These episodes were audibly in the background as Carney delineated the reasons that Europeans and Canadians want to draw together “so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law”. Other misadventures this week reveal how the strategy of demeaning allies is backfiring badly. For some time, Trump has been badgering South Korea for assistance, while scaling back US military support there, and bizarrely claiming that North Korea, a far greater nuclear threat than Iran, is “unthreatening and respectful”. Unsurprisingly, South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, announced on Friday that he would not send troops or military assets to support Trump’s war of choice in Iran. Back in Trump’s America, the war continues to drive up gas prices. That’s in addition to the ongoing expenses created by Trump’s endless tariffs, keenly felt in the very states that are closest to Canada. They include Michigan, a battleground state where families now face the highest tariff burden in the US, $5,600 per household since the “golden age” began in January 2025. It is difficult to see how this ends well for the embattled president, making enemies at home and around the world, less than two months before the midterms. Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

webTitle: The US supreme court issued a fragile win for voting rights – the real test comes later | Claire Finkelstein

fields.headline: The US supreme court issued a fragile win for voting rights – the real test comes later
fields.trailText: The court’s decision was based entirely on the timing of proposed new mail-in ballot rules. The larger question could re-emerge
fields.bodyText: Last week’s supreme court decision upholding the district court’s restraining order on USPS’s mail-in ballot restrictions is being hailed as a victory for electoral integrity by politicians, political commentators and voting rights advocates alike. The senator Chuck Schumer, for example, called the decision “one of the most important cases to protect voting rights before the supreme court”. But the unsigned, three-sentence opinion, with only a brief concurrence and a lengthy dissent, is no such thing. The court based its brief opinion entirely on the timing of the roll-out of the new rules, which became effective on 21 August, just weeks away from the midterm elections and only days before several states were scheduled to begin mailing out their ballots. California’s submission to the court, joined by twenty-two states and the district of Columbia, asking the court to leave the injunction against the rule change in place, made clear that compliance with the rules in advance of the midterms would not only be difficult; it would be impossible without disenfranchising thousands of voters. And that, of course, is the point. The court fight over the timing of the rule change does not address whether USPS has a right to burden mail-in voting to this degree in the first place. By statute, USPS is permitted to promulgate rules governing the mail, and the substantive question about the enactment of these rules after the elections will be whether they exceed that statutory permission or are otherwise unconstitutional. This was the message of the justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence. Even though he agreed that insisting on implementing the new rules prior to the midterms would be “arbitrary and capricious”, he evinced no objection to the rules change when time permits. It will presumably fall to the court after the midterms to determine whether the new rules are a permissible response to concerns about electoral security or whether they primarily serve the impermissible purpose of restricting the franchise. In addition to the Kavanaugh concurrence, the justice Samuel Alito, in his dissent joined by the justice Clarence Thomas, was adamant that the USPS had every right to enact the intended rules change, even prior to the midterms, under the general powers of the post office under federal law. It was hard not to be struck by the irony that these two stalwart supporters of presidential powers, Alito and Thomas, would find themselves suddenly defending the autonomy of an independent agency based on deference to congressional legislation and the value of separation of powers, when in other cases, such as Seila law v CFPB, they set themselves against Congress’s delegation of authority to an independent agency precisely on separation of powers grounds. It is surely not a coincidence that presidential powers are enhanced by Congress’s delegation to the agency in the former case but weakened by a comparable delegation in the latter case. Whether they say so explicitly or not, these two justices increasingly divide up the landscape as a struggle between presidential power on the one hand versus anything that might infringe on that power on the other. Whether the issue is the president’s right to regulate the mail; his right to remove heads of agencies, including supposedly independent agencies; his right to claim executive privilege over communications with advisers; or even his right to commit crimes with impunity through the vehicle of his official duties, Alito and Thomas, joined frequently by other members of the court’s conservative majority, have increasingly allowed their jurisprudence to be held prisoner by the drive to expand presidential authority. But not all instances of presidential authority. Thomas’s concurring opinion in Trump v United States, which established immunity to prosecution for crimes the president performs in his official capacity, argued that Jack Smith’s prosecution of Trump violated the appointments clause of article II, section 2, clause 2, which he characterizes as “an important check against the president” – in this case, Joe Biden. Apparently the appointments clause is singular in establishing a constraint on presidential authority, while Thomas refuses to recognize most other such constraints where the presidential authority in question is Trump’s. Thus whether it is Congress’s power of the purse (see the tariff decision), the president’s rights over immigration (see the Haitian immigrants’ case) or his 91-page dissenting opinion in Trump v Barbara attacking the majority’s rejection of the president’s power to eliminate the 14th amendment’s guarantee of birthright citizenship (Trump v Barbara) – none of these possible constraints struck Thomas as valid. But the appointments clause is? Trump’s remarks about Monday’s ruling, which he characterized as a “big loss for Republicans”, seem to confirm that the president’s primary purpose in demanding the new rules is voter suppression. The real question is whether the USPS must or even may allow itself to be used for partisan political purposes when election regulation is beyond its mandate. States regulate elections, not the postal service. The new rules may therefore violate principles of federalism even when enacted with plenty of time for states to comply. The court’s opinion does not tell us one way or another whether the three justices clearly supportive of the rules change would be joined by any other justices. Defenders of voting rights must not relax. While USPS v California is a temporary political setback for the president and his fellow Republicans, it is not yet a home run for democracy. Claire Finkelstein, a contributing opinion writer to the Guardian, is the Algernon Biddle professor of law and professor of philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania and the faculty director of its Center for Ethics and the Rule of Law

webTitle: All the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it now | Larry Elliott

fields.headline: All the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it now
fields.trailText: War, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help us, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
fields.bodyText: Bad stuff happens in September. For some reason, it is a month that has had more than its fair share of financial crises, perhaps because problems that have been bubbling away come into sharper focus once the summer holidays are over. Britain came off the Gold Standard in September 1931. The pound was turfed out of Europe’s Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992. And 18 years ago this week, the collapse of Lehman Brothers plunged the global economy into deep recession. This September, there are again reasons to be nervous. There are soaring oil prices, which are feeding through into higher petrol and diesel prices, adding to cost of living pressures. There is a sell-off in government bonds around the world. There is the warning from AI bosses that it would be wise to slow the pace of development in their industry. Mixed together, they are the ingredients for another troubled September. Of course, it may all be a false alarm. It is now more than six months since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran and so far the impact of closing the strait of Hormuz has been far less severe than was expected back in the spring. It is possible the fear currently gripping bond markets will quickly pass, especially if the wars in Ukraine and Iran end soon. The constant refrain from Donald Trump that oil tankers will soon be passing unhindered once again through the strait of Hormuz has limited the rise in crude prices. Growth has not been hit that much, and in both the US and the UK, AI has been part of that story. There are, though, signs that the war in Iran is having an effect, albeit with a longer lag than originally expected. Markets no longer believe Trump when he says a deal with Iran is about to be clinched. As a result, the rise in oil prices to more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks has heightened fears of persistent inflation and of higher interest rates from central banks. And despite crude prices not escalating, the cost of petrol and diesel remains high, thanks to a shortage of refining capacity. For months, share prices have been underpinned by the belief that there is no ceiling on the growth of technology stocks, particularly those involved in AI. That theory is now being tested and as far as Wall Street is concerned, the recent intervention by the AI bosses was spectacularly ill-timed. Trump’s rejection of the need for tighter regulation on the AI industry speaks volumes. This is only partly to do with the US-China battle to win the technology war. Financial markets now look as fragile as they have been at any time since September 2008, and with US midterm elections looming, the president needs to prevent the AI-led stock market bubble from popping. History never repeats itself exactly. There are similarities between September 2026 and September 2008, but there are differences too. The crash of 2008 was the result of banks over-reaching themselves to finance US real estate. The banks seem to be far less exposed this time, and while some of the investment in technology stocks may have been predicated on unrealistic assumptions about future profits, AI is clearly going to have a positive long-term economic impact in a way that the investment in housing pre-2008 did not. It is wrong to think all bubbles are the same. That said, there are lessons to be learned from the events of 2008. One is that if a financial crisis morphs into an economic slump – as it did 18 years ago – then orthodoxy goes out of the window. There will be no more talk of interest-rate increases from central banks or of the need for finance ministries to slash budget deficits. Indeed, the recent bond buybacks by the US treasury, which were designed to reduce the upward pressure on mortgage interest rates, car loans and credit card debt, were both an indication of how nervous the Trump administration is about the current state of financial markets and a taste of the more vigorous intervention that a full-blown financial crisis would prompt. An even bigger lesson is the need to control what happens after a crash. Last time, the left was caught unawares and allowed the right to seize the initiative. Already there are signs in Britain of the same dynamic, with the chancellor, John Healey, coming under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending in next month’s budget. This would be self-defeating, not least because it would run counter to Andy Burnham’s (to my mind, entirely correct) argument that 40 years of neoliberalism was a mistake that needs rectifying. It would also come at a time when – as this week’s TUC conference in Brighton showed – there is genuine support on the left for a comprehensive strategy to re-industrialise Britain. A range of trade unions – Unite, RMT, CWU, GMB and Equity – made it clear at the conference that they wanted a much more interventionist approach, and a collection of essays, to which I contributed, has just been published, fleshing out what Burnham would need to do to make good on his re-industrialisation pledge. If not now, then sooner or later there will be another financial crisis. People forget. They become complacent. They overlook the strains in financial markets that have been allowed to become too big and too powerful. So while recent events may blow over, it would also be sensible to plan for another September meltdown. Just in case. Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

webTitle: Monday briefing: Inside Trump’s deportation machine – ‘Your fate is out of your control’

fields.headline: Monday briefing: Inside Trump’s deportation machine – ‘Your fate is out of your control’
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: The US administration has built a system of removing migrants to countries they have no connection with, often with little warning
fields.bodyText: Good morning. If you want to grasp the true cost of what it means to “secure our borders,” skip the panicked headlines about “mega-dinghies” arriving on British shores and the pictures of Patriot Platform’s black-clad enthusiasts, and look across the Atlantic. Since 2025, the Trump administration has deported about 5,000 people on flights to “third countries” where they have no family ties or history, sometimes as far as Ghana and Sierra Leone. A Guardian investigation published today exposes the staggering cruelty of this sinister policy. It seems deliberately designed to stoke fear, and shows how far-right ideas that once belonged on the fringes of politics have become so mainstream that they’re now barely opposed. These deportations often happen very quickly, with people given little notice of what is going to happen to them. That creates huge challenges for lawyers trying to defend people who are shackled on flights, and for journalists trying to tell their stories. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s investigations correspondent Louisa Loveluck about the lives of the people caught up in this policy, and how the Trump administration has created a deportation machine. That’s after the headlines. Weekend roundup Russia | European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”. Domestic violence | About 20,000 disclosures of domestic abuse are estimated to be made to maternity services in England every year, analysis has found. Ed Sheeran | Ed Sheeran has opened a solo concert in Philadelphia with comments about Gaza, saying what is happening is “catastrophic and unjustifiable”, in his first show since his tour was plunged into turmoil. Spycops scandal | Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers. Royal family | Earl Spencer has said the relationship between the press and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex “echoes” the way the media treated his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC aired on Sunday evening, Spencer described media coverage of Harry and Meghan as having a “cancerous influence”. In depth: The people caught in Trump’s deportation machine The second Trump administration has struck 35 deals with nations such as Eswatini and Central African Republic, allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to nations where they have no connections. Federal officers can deport immigrants with as little as six hours notice, even if they have no assurances that people will be safe from persecution or torture (a US court judgment recently challenged the short timeframe, and the government is expected to appeal it). In many cases, these countries then deport people onwards to the places they fled – something that is technically illegal under US law. Since 2025, more than 5,000 people have been put on planes to countries other than their own, including those in Latin America, Africa, central Asia and the Caribbean. Louisa has been investigating these deportations with journalists from 22 other newsrooms in conjunction with Forbidden Stories, a Paris-based network of investigative journalists. One of the people they interviewed was Rabbiatu Kuyateh, a 58-year-old nurse who had been living in the US for 30 years. During the pandemic, Kuyateh said she had spent much of the pandemic working in a US hospital caring for patients in a Covid isolation ward. Since then, she has worked as a carer for the disabled son of an American family. She was detained during a routine check-in with ICE in July 2025, spent four months in ICE custody, and was then flown to Ghana. Days later, a group of officials dragged her by her hair into a van, which transported her to Sierra Leone, the country she had originally fled with her parents. “The disabled man who Kuyateh was paid to care for was waiting for her on the day she was picked up by ICE,” Louisa says. “And when she could finally speak to her family after she was detained, one of the things she said was: please tell them I’m not coming to work tomorrow.” *** Who is behind this? The policy has been driven by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who is often described as Trump’s “shadow president”. During Trump’s first term, Miller was behind the administration’s most extreme positions, such as the Muslim travel ban. In November 2024, before returning to the White House, he said on a conservative radio show that the coming crackdown on immigrants would be so prolific, “you’ll set your alarm clock two hours earlier every morning just to get two more hours of daylight to watch the deportation flights happen.” Since then, he’s been in overdrive. Miller has demanded that ICE agents arrest 3,000 people per day on America’s streets, and has strategised with officials from the Department of Homeland Security about how the government can reach its goal of deporting one million people in a year. He hosts daily calls with a small circle of conservative diplomats to press them on third country deportation agreements, and has been trying to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US. His influence is part of a broader strategy to subordinate the federal government’s other priorities to the singular aim of deporting migrants. The Trump administration has disbanded USAID, and repurposed funding previously dedicated to humanitarian assistance towards deportations. It has purged immigration judges deemed insufficiently loyal to this agenda, and has gutted the oversight system that investigates civil rights abuses in immigration detention. “All of these institutions that on some level could have protected refugees, asylum seekers and migrants are being turned inside out to do the opposite,” Louisa says. *** Why the Trump administration doesn’t want you to know the details Trump has made no secret of his gigantic deportation programme (it will be a “bloody story,” he said in 2024). His government has transformed immigration raids into reality entertainment, staged photo ops at migrant detention jails with names such as Deportation Depot and Alligator Alcatraz, and in 2025 arrested two firefighters while they were putting out an active wildfire in Washington State, later deporting one of them to Mexico. But it has been comparatively guarded about its third-party deportation deals. Details of the deals remain opaque, and the government doesn’t publicise most of the deportation flights. Secrecy makes it harder for lawyers to oppose deportations, since they often don’t know when flights are scheduled – or who is on them. It also contributes to a climate of fear and uncertainty for immigrants. “The message is: you are out of control of your own fate,” Louisa tells me. The countries that have struck these deals with the US may not want them to be public knowledge, and by keeping them out of the public eye, the Trump administration can also limit scrutiny of how much they cost. So far, it has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure these agreements. The cost of deporting a single person can run as high as $1m. “The administration seems willing to pay whatever it takes to get this done,” Louisa says. (When approached for comment, a state department spokesperson said the administration would use “all legal means” to remove those “with no right to remain in our country”.) *** From far-right conspiracy to government policy The policy is being run from the newly created Office of Remigration, which has borrowed a term used by the far-right to describe the forcible expulsion of immigrants, turning an idea once associated with the political fringes into official government policy. The idea that people who have been living in a country legally for years could be deported in the space of a few hours might sound like dystopian fiction. But as my colleague Jonathan Liew wrote in an opinion piece last year, the remigration discourse has already gone mainstream. In 2022, the UK’s then Conservative government attempted its own version of the third country deportation policy by pushing through plans to send migrants to Rwanda (the first flight was cancelled after a flurry of legal challenges). Reform has now proposed that, if it were to form a government, people who have already secured indefinite leave to remain could be suddenly deported if they don’t meet a new set of rules. And, as we reported yesterday, Nigel Farage has said he would like to “hijack” Trump’s key ICE adviser to secure the UK’s borders. “This is not just an American policy,” Louisa tells me. “This is the language of our political debate right now. And if America is doing this so flagrantly, it makes it easier for others to do the same.” We want to hear from you What do you want to know about the US midterms, and how the Guardian plans to report them? Libby will be putting your questions to our Washington bureau in the coming weeks, so send them in by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com. The week to come Monday | G7’s foreign ministers are set to meet in New York. Wednesday | The disgraced film tycoon Harvey Weinstein is set to face his fourth and possibly final sentencing in New York for sexually assaulting a former assistant. Thursday | US president Donald Trump is set to host Xi Jinping, China’s president, at the White House. What else we’ve been enjoying I loved this interview with Ms Rachel, the toddler whisperer extraordinaire, about being a campaigner on humanitarian issues, politics, and her new album “I’m So Happy”. Sundus Abdi, newsletters team I appreciated this analysis by David Smith on Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Centre after himself. On the US president’s motivations, lawyer Norm Eisen said: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question.” Micha Frazer-Carroll, newsletters team What comforted Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe while she was imprisoned in an Iranian jail? Pizza dough, Zumba and sewing, she tells reporter Helena Horton. Sundus Sport Football | Matheus Cunha’s late equaliser gave Manchester United a 1-1 draw at Fulham, who had led through Lisandro Martínez’s farcical own goal. Cycling | Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel won the men’s time trial title for the fourth time in a row, while the Swiss rider Marlen Reusser defended her women’s crown. Darts | Luke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. The front pages “European spy chiefs brace for Russia to test Nato pact”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Labour eyes £14bn tax raid to help the poorest”, the Times says “Half Labour MPs at risk of Pip cuts backlash”, and the Express writes “Stop your tax raid on nation’s high streets”. The Mail runs with “Kemi: I’ll ditch tourist tax to boost Britain” and the i Paper has “We women are all at risk from men, warns minister amid Piddington asylum camp row”. The FT says “BigTech banks of guarantees to keep $300bn AI exposure off balance sheet”. The Mirror’s splash is “Ed: I feel so alone” and Metro writes “I back Team Harry AND Wills” Today in Focus Being trans in Britain in 2026 Transgender people in Britain are navigating a new reality. In August, new guidance – in the form of a document nearly 350 pages long – was published to help institutions interpret last year’s supreme court ruling on trans rights. It means, as Amelia outlines to Helen Pidd, that every time she goes to a pub or restaurant, she is terrified about going to the bathroom. Helen heads to parliament to hear from those protesting over the new guidance, and from senior political correspondent Peter Walker on whether there is any appetite in government to change the law. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad For decades, hopeful entrants to the Royal Horticultural Society’s Britain in Bloom competition have nurtured vibrant flowerbeds and beautiful hanging baskets across the UK’s towns. This year, the charity has launched a new award that has zhooshed up many of our train platforms. Five of the best were shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition – featuring boat-planters, pollination-friendly wildflowers and gravel gardens. The winner, the Cardross Community Organic Garden in Scotland, involved a wide range of local communities in gardening activities, from Brownies to volunteering groups. Jane Connolly, who heads the station’s gardening group, said: “Every time we are down there, somebody will come along and peruse it and say how grateful they are with what we have done … People come to our station just to see our gardens.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

webTitle: Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage

fields.headline: Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage
fields.trailText: While world leaders prepare for annual UN gathering, shifts in the global order continue in the face of a disruptive American president
fields.bodyText: In the event of a midterms election battering, it is possible that a deflated Donald Trump, constrained by a Democrat-controlled Congress, will gradually have to face up to the indignity of irrelevance. While continuing to sign off Truth Social posts with his usual, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, no one will actually be paying much attention. His meandering press conferences will no longer be carried live by TV networks. The Republican party will move on to the question of his successor. Trump could announce he had changed the name of the Champs-Élysées to Sunset Boulevard and even Google Maps will stifle a yawn. He would become that most pitied of political animals, the lame duck. Yet somehow this scenario does not seem to fit the Trump personality, the US media landscape or indeed the recent history of other presidential endings. Just before completing their own terms in office, George W Bush launched the Iraq war “surge”, Bill Clinton got China into the World Trade Organization and Ronald Reagan helped end the cold war. Trump will also surely rage against the dying of the light. Many observers, including the former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton and the former UK foreign secretary David Lammy, predict Trump will concentrate even more on his disruptive foreign policy after November’s midterms, seeking to go even further and faster. Potential legislative gridlock in Congress would block him off from domestic initiatives, so the thinking goes, but much less so foreign policy. The likes of António Guterres, attending his final UN general assembly as secretary general this week, who have tried to impress on Trump that the US could achieve more in alliance with others than alone, are likely to receive short shrift. Those hoping for a return from the orderless world to one of order, loosely built around a set of recognisable values, are likely to be disappointed. In short, there is more to come. *** That assessment is accelerating a trend across the world of countries forming a complex web of diplomatic, military and trading alliances designed to act as protective shields from an unpredictable and predatory US president. These hedging alliances, born out of fear of entrapment or of abandonment, are springing up across the globe, changing the matrix of diplomacy, often but not always in favour of the other superpower of the age, China. John Bew, a foreign policy adviser to four former British prime ministers, describes the process as the creation of “a sub-threshold international order”. As Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, urged in a speech at Davos in January, the middle powers are reorganising. The trend is most obvious among former US allies. Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, said: “The world is moving from a situation where countries saw themselves within the context of an alliance system – ‘How do we plug and play and make it all about interoperability with American grand strategy?’ – towards one where the primary goal is: ’How do we hedge and how do we make sure that we can defend ourselves if America isn’t there?’” Wherever one looks it is the alliances in which the US does not feature – from Brics to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) – that are thriving and deepening. The recent Brics summit in Delhi ended with a declaration 140 dense paragraphs long that centred on how sovereign states can insulate their economies, supply lines, and payment infrastructures from weaponised western financial networks. The aim was to show that the “global south” can shape rules without turning into an anti-American alliance. “The operational strategy does not aim to eradicate the dollar overnight,” the Indian commentator Navroop Singh explained, “but to construct a parallel, non-dollar pipeline through which bilateral commerce, especially in strategic commodities like oil, gas, agriculture, and critical minerals can flow unhindered by extraterritorial oversight of the United States.” At this month’s SCO meeting at Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan, China’s president, Xi Jinping, said: “The overwhelming majority of countries do not subscribe to power politics, do not want conflict and confrontation, and do not wish to remain closed off and left behind. Instead, they aspire to secure an equal place on the world stage through their own development and international cooperation.” Formed to manage border disputes among former Soviet states, the SCO’s activities long ago expanded to include an economic dimension fostering connectivity, trade and investment. By contrast, in the groupings that the US dominates, such as the G7 and Nato, the recent key ambition has been to shape an agenda that avoids a Trump walkout. Success is measured according to whether the west avoids public disintegration. Sometimes these new ad hoc alliances are relatively mundane. Some operate inside existing institutions, others involve the creation of specific new cooperation trading mechanisms such as memorandums of understanding on trade in critical minerals or the development of new overlapping institutions. In the case of the UK, the Chatham House thinktank suggests as many as six different mini-alliances could be formed to build submarines and air engines, share critical minerals, or promote free trade. *** The biggest and most striking recent manifestation of this new order came in the Middle East on 7 August, when Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca pact – a defensive military alliance that for some is about ending the dependency on the US military umbrella, and for others combatting Iran. Either way, it is likely to rewrite the Middle East’s security architecture. Trita Parsi, from the US foreign policy thinktank the Quincy Institute For Responsible Statecraft, said: “If you sit in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries right now, you must feel tremendously vulnerable because you have put all your eggs in the American security basket and it turned out not only not to work, but it was supposed to be a guarantee that others would be deterred from attacking you. Instead, the US started a war against the wishes of most Gulf countries and within that war, the entire infrastructure of the US bases turned out not to be a deterrent, but a magnet.” Not only were exposed bases pummelled by Iranian missiles and drones to the point, in the words of Gen David Petraeus, that they became “no longer viable”, the Gulf states also discovered the US was prepared to allow Israel to bomb Qatar’s capital, Doha, in the hope of assassinating the Hamas leadership. It was the first such attack on a GCC state, and changed the GCC’s security calculations as to whether Iran or Israel ultimately was the primary threat in the region. The US insists in public it will reinvest in better-protected bases and will shortly lay out a postwar vision in which the US remains indispensable to the Gulf’s security. But Majed al-Ansari, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Gulf nations cannot rely solely on the US and other international alliances for their security. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward.” Parsi admitted it was not clear what kind of tree would grow out of the seed sown in Mecca. “Is it another bloc formation that at its core divides the region, leading to rivalry and confrontation, or is it, as the Turks insist, an open constellation that is not targeting anyone but based on collective security?” Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, meanwhile, requires foreign investment, tourism and reliable energy routes. Endless wars promoted by Israel and not constrained by the US for purposes not in Saudi Arabia’s long-term interest are a ball and chain on the Saudi economy. In all this, there are deep implications for India, a country dependent on the Middle East for nearly 60% of its crude oil and about 70% of its liquefied natural gas requirements. It may need to form its own hard power security partnerships in the region. Writing in Foreign Affairs magazine, Marc Lynch, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University, asked recently: “If Washington could not even be counted on to consult its allies, defeat its adversaries, or protect its partners from the fallout of its regional misadventures, then what good were its promises? The fundamental bargain the United States offered has crumbled, and it will not be easily rebuilt”. The same set of questions has been posed in Europe, leading to calls for a more Europeanised Nato, most often perceived as an alliance of its five main military powers, a constellation that conveniently bypasses Brexit and would allow Germany, France, Italy, Poland and the UK to work together to face the Russian threat, assuming these democracies next year remain led by forces opposed to Putin’s authoritarianism. Debate about this alliance, promoted at the Munich Security Conference, is driven by the twin fears of the hybrid war conducted by Moscow and the US plan to leave the conventional defence of Europe to the Europeans. Trumpites treat Europeans primarily as trade competitors and sometimes a civilisational threat, not allies. No one can assume that the US would come to Europe’s defence in the event of a Russian attack. Not surprisingly, Poland, the Baltics and Scandinavia have since 2022 increased their defence spending by 71%, 134% and 126% respectively. The call to buy European arms is growing. Such is the concern about where Trump could go next after his threats to Greenland, that some European diplomats privately express relief that the US was unable to repeat the success of Venezuela in Iran. There is no love for the Iranian government, save for its ability to remind Europe of the risks inherent in relying on US military and technological supremacy. *** The country that most acutely faces the American dilemma is of course Canada. Now entering an asymmetric trade war with the largest and most powerful country in the world, it has little doubt about the rupture it is confronting. Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the UN, recently wrote: “Canada’s nextdoor neighbour is a predatory hegemon [that] tears up treaties, makes a mockery of international law and clearly has a different concept of the relationships between might and right, and between law, morality and self-interest.” But there was an ambiguity deep in Carney’s Davos message. Was he seeking simply to locate new markets blocked by US tariffs, or was he trying to build a network of countries – a third bloc – with like-minded liberal values? Rae argued that for the middle nations alliance to thrive, Carney needed to be clearer about what values Canada stands for, including upholding international law. He wrote: “We can succeed in defeating such aggression only if we are willing to extend economic, political and military support to other countries and jurisdictions facing similar attacks and threats.” In his speech to the European parliament this week while trying to provide the cure to the harsh realities his Davos speech diagnosed, Carney argued that associate membership of the EU would not just be about economics, but an affinity of deep-rooted shared values that implicitly Canada no longer shared with the US. But the rules-based EU does not give access to its markets readily, and the big vision could soon become entangled in the small print Brussels adores. Sometimes this crisis of the west is seen as an exclusively European phenomenon. But South Korea finds itself in a similar place to Canada. Ulchi Freedom Shield, the annual joint military exercise that the US and South Korea held to counter the North Korean threat, was abruptly scaled back by Washington just before it was due to begin in August. Trump ordered the drills cut from 11 days to five, citing costs, his desire to improve relations with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s reluctance to support his war on Iran. The decline in US military stocks due to the Iran war has hardly helped. It has intensified a debate in South Korea, and in Japan, about pursuing independent nuclear weapons, especially given the apparent indifference of the US and the international community to North Korea’s programme. The friction has given Xi a golden opportunity to promote China to South Korea and Asia as the more reliable ally. Optimists such as Kurt Campbell, who under Joe Biden’s presidency latterly as deputy secretary of state did more than anyone to reconstruct American alliances across Asia after the Trump first term, insists his task can be repeated. There is no need to panic, he said, arguing that “by the winter there will be a dramatic resurgence in discussion, debate, hope and, frankly, optimism about what comes next”. The old centrifugal forces including European aversion to Chinese protectionism and US dominance in artificial intelligence, will resurface. The counterview is that something fundamental has changed. Once bitten, twice shy, the old transatlantic order will not be restored, and something new, less predictable, more fragmented is already taking shape.
